name: PT Argha Karya Prima Industry Tbk

frontmatter.title: Argha Karya Prima — the half-year stub, the bridge, and a target that survives both
frontmatter.summary: The fatal point was the mechanism, not the size: the DCF counted half of a full-year cash flow whose working-capital build fell entirely in the first half. We rebase working capital to the June balance sheet, bridge the second-half cash flow and mark the associate at its sale price. Base equity roughly doubles; the target falls as the bull case pays for the same working capital. SELL, target Rp90.
thesis: The stub was wrong and is now bridged: rebasing working capital to the 30 June balance sheet and adding the second-half cash flow the discount stub omits roughly doubles the base equity value to Rp109, while the higher working-capital requirement cuts the bull case and the target to Rp90 [S3, S4].

The market still pays for the spike: net of the associate at the observable sale price the market enterprise value is about two fifths above the DCF's IDR1,223.5bn, an implied terminal margin a shade above the FY2022 peak that no filed note supports [S0, S3, F32].
The cash flow contradicts the profit: first-half operating cash flow was IDR-146.7bn against net profit of IDR66.2bn, funded by IDR1,016.6bn of annually renewable short-term lines [S3, F35, F39].

The dividend is funded where it is paid: the model pays each distribution a year after the profit, so the Rp101 a share from FY2026E is covered by FY2027E free cash flow to equity of IDR167.8bn [S4, F20].

The associate is the only positive piece of the equity value and the company has already sold part of it once; a further disposal at the sale price is a bear-case event, not a hidden asset [S3, F37, F38, F52].

blocks.text: **What this revision changes.** The red team's fatal challenge was right about the mechanism and wrong about the size. The engine discounts the rest of FY2026E by taking the whole year's free cash flow and multiplying it by the part of the year left after 30 June — a hair over half. That is a fair stub only if the cash is earned evenly. Here the entire working-capital build of IDR383.2bn fell in the first half: the half consumed IDR-146.7bn of operating cash and IDR45.3bn plus IDR22.8bn of capex, so the annual free cash flow of IDR-138.8bn is far more negative than the second half will be [S3, F35, F50, F51]. We fix it in two sourced places: working capital is rebased to the 30 June balance sheet so FY2026E carries neither a second-half build nor a second-half release, and the gap between the true second-half cash flow and the stub is a bridge line. The associate is marked at the January sale price instead of book. Base equity value rises from the thin sliver of the last version to Rp109 a share; the target falls to Rp90 because the working capital that makes the second half cash-positive has to be funded, which cuts the bull case, and because the distribution is now shown as the ex-dividend deduction it is [S3, S4]. This round also removes the associate income the earlier forecast carried: FY2026E operating profit is IDR251.3bn, the film-only run-rate of twice the half-year print less the associate line, not the associate-inclusive IDR129.9bn annualised, so the stake is counted once, in the bridge [S3, F12, F36].

The sixfold understatement the challenge computed does not survive the reconciliation: its starting point was the previous FY2026E free cash flow of a small positive number, which was itself built on a working-capital assumption the June balance sheet contradicts. Once the build is in the annual figure the first period of the DCF is deeply negative and the second half is strongly positive; the net correction raises the base equity value roughly twofold and lowers the bull case [S3, S4].

**SELL, target Rp90, -70.7% expected total return.** Argha converts imported polymer into biaxially oriented film at Citeureup and sells it to food, beverage and consumer-goods packagers [S2]. It runs 113,000 tonnes of BOPP and 13,000 tonnes of BOPET, with a 7,200 tonne CPP line under construction, inside a 154,200 tonne total that includes 21,000 tonnes at an equity-accounted associate [S2, S3]. It earned almost nothing for three years; 2026 turned the feedstock spike into profit, though not yet into cash [S3].

The variant view is the opposite of the obvious one: the market is not treating the spike as temporary, it is capitalising it. At Rp650 the enterprise value net of the associate is about two fifths above the DCF's IDR1,223.5bn on a like-for-like basis, which needs a terminal reported gross margin a shade above the FY2022 peak against an audited 11.0% in FY2025 [S0, S4, S2, F32]. What is left for the equity is the associate plus the two bridge corrections, and none of it is operating [S3, F37, F38].

Three things move the value, and the first two move it down. The terminal spread is the whole call: a point of terminal gross margin takes the twelve-month value from Rp25 to many times itself, and a point below base is already nil (fund record sensitivity grid). Cash conversion is the second: FY2025 operating cash flow of IDR221.2bn against net profit of IDR12.7bn was unusually good, and the first half of 2026 reverses it [S4, S3]. Liquidity is the third and it is mechanical: the target is the weighted value less the tier discount, and the measured traded value sits a few per cent above the tier that halves it [S0]. The distribution is not a fourth: it is paid a year after the profit that funds it, and the total return adds it back [S4, F20].

The bear case is not a liquidation and the bull case is not a melt-up. The bear takes the margin down a point and a half and revenue growth down four points, which floors the equity at zero through the debt; the bull mirrors the same two shocks upward as the CPP line ramps, which is roughly where the market trades today [S3, S4]. The base case is the last audited margin on the house deck — the most likely path, not the cautious one: it assumes the feedstock normalises with the deck, not that it collapses.

Argha runs one consolidated site and sells plain and metallised BOPP, BOPET for lidding and industrial uses, and CPP for laminates, moving toward higher-barrier film rather than commodity plain film [S2]. The 21,000 tonnes in Malaysia belong to Stenta Films, a Malaysian producer in which Argha retained a minority after selling part of its stake in January 2026 [S3]. The company sold that stake to Mega First Corporation Berhad at RM1.28 a share and received IDR114.9bn on 9 February 2026 [S3, p46, F38]. The retained interest is equity-accounted and its profit is printed inside the group's operating profit; the model strips it out of the forecast operating profit and values the stake separately in the bridge rather than inside the DCF, so the earnings and the asset are counted once each [S3, note 2g, F36, F37].

The business model is a conversion spread. The company buys polymer resin, mostly imported, melts and stretches it, and sells film by the tonne at a price negotiated with a lag against the resin price [S4, S6]. Raw materials were IDR1,869.7bn of IDR2,614.9bn of cost of goods sold in FY2025, about seven tenths, so the cost base is exposed to oil and the rupiah through naphtha [S4, S6]. The skill is in film specification and the speed of the price reset, not the molecule. Exports were IDR865.2bn of IDR1,754.8bn of first-half sales, just under half, and no single customer was above a tenth [S3, S4]. FY2025 capital expenditure was IDR284.4bn plus IDR62.7bn of advances, above depreciation, because CPP and metallising capacity were being built [S4, F8, F9].

Flexible-packaging film is a regional price-following business: demand grows with food and consumer volumes, but supply is lumpy because a new line is a multi-year project, so the spread cycles with capacity additions rather than demand [S2, S6]. The upcycle is cost-driven: polypropylene rose by more than two fifths year on year, led by naphtha [S5, S6]. A converter that resets quickly earns a wider absolute spread on a higher cost base, but the percentage only expands if the gap per tonne widens or the mix improves [S3, S4].

The policy backdrop has turned supportive, but by less than the headline suggests. A finance-minister regulation in October 2026 granted a zero per cent import duty on six polymer tariff lines for six months [S5]. The imports covered are mostly liquid forms rather than the polymer pellets a film converter buys, and no pre-relief rate is published, so we do not turn the regulation into a point estimate: a point of duty on the imported polymer share is about one part in seventy-five of gross profit, and the extension sits in the bull narrative [S4, S5, F15]. The risk is that it expires [S5].

Competition is regional and the moat is narrow but real. Integrated producers in Thailand, Malaysia and China make both film and resin and can undercut a non-integrated converter when resin is cheap and the rupiah is strong; Argha's defence is customer qualification, metallising capability and the associate's regional access [S2, S6]. A new entrant needs a line, a qualification and a formulation, which takes years, but with no feedstock integration supplier power is high and buyer power moderate [S2, S4]. Brent runs from US$92.1/bbl spot to US$96.0/bbl in FY2026E and US$84.0/bbl in FY2027E, the single most important external variable for the spread, while the macro deck carries the rupiah at Rp18,350/USD against a spot of Rp18,228/USD [S4, S6].

The history is a converter that lost its spread in the downcycle and has recovered it. Revenue was IDR3,105.6bn in FY2022, IDR2,723.6bn in FY2023, IDR3,025.0bn in FY2024 and IDR2,938.7bn in FY2025; gross profit went from IDR375.0bn to IDR225.0bn and IDR323.8bn, a margin of 11.0% [S0, S4, S2]. Operating profit collapsed to IDR16.1bn and recovered to IDR97.7bn, still below FY2022 [S0, S4]. The swing is the spread, not volume [S4].

The first half of 2026 is the inflection. Revenue was IDR1,754.8bn, gross profit IDR228.4bn, operating profit IDR129.9bn and net profit IDR66.2bn against a loss a year earlier [S3]. The gross margin expanded by nearly three points because the absolute spread per tonne widened and the mix moved toward metallised film, both cyclical in a business with no feedstock integration [S3, S4].

The accounts need two restatements, not one. The data pack carried a depreciation charge of only a few billion rupiah for FY2025, a fragment of the real charge; the fixed-asset note shows IDR164.8bn in FY2025 and IDR153.0bn in FY2024, and the audited income statement shows operating profit of IDR97.7bn and IDR110.4bn against the pack's lower figures [S4, F8, F9]. The second is the associate: the printed operating profit includes the associate's share, contrary to the accounting-policy note. The half year builds IDR129.9bn as IDR228.4bn of gross profit plus IDR4.4bn of associate income less selling and administrative costs and other income, and FY2025's IDR97.7bn likewise contains IDR13.0bn [S3, p6, F6, F11, F12, F36, F45]. The forecast must strip that income out: the SG&A input is struck on the film-only cost base, so FY2026E operating profit is IDR251.3bn, the film-only run-rate of twice the half-year print less twice the associate line, not the associate-inclusive figure. The stake is then valued once, in the equity bridge, and the earnings and the asset are not double counted. On the earnings-quality test the clean operating profit is lower than the printed figure by about a thirtieth in the half year and about an eighth in FY2025, and the calibration comparison of the FY2025 margin with the FY2026E forecast carries that difference as well as the cyclical recovery [S3, S4].

The forecast follows the last actual and the deck. FY2026E revenue is IDR3,497.1bn, growth of 19.0%, because the first half is booked and the second half is set at the first-half run-rate [S3]. FY2027E falls -6.0% as Brent normalises from US$96.0/bbl to US$84.0/bbl and the selling price deflates with resin [S4, S2]. The gross-margin input is 14.3% at FY2025 input costs, which the Brent link takes to a reported 13.0%; from FY2027E the margin is 12.5% and settles at about 11.0%, the FY2025 audited 11.0% and below the FY2022 peak, because no filed note quantifies a mix uplift [S3, S2, F32, S4]. SG&A is 5.9% of revenue and drifts to 6.2% against a largely fixed cost base [S3, S4].

Free cash flow is the point of this revision. FY2026E operating profit is IDR251.3bn, EBITDA IDR443.6bn, capex IDR136.4bn and the working-capital build IDR383.2bn, so annual free cash flow is IDR-138.8bn and FY2027E is IDR235.5bn [S4, S3, F35]. That annual figure is not earned evenly: the first half consumed IDR-146.7bn of operating cash and IDR45.3bn plus IDR22.8bn of capex, and the whole working-capital build was a first-half event, so the second half generates most of the year. The second-half assumption is explicit and deliberately neutral: FY2026E operating working capital is pinned to the 30 June level, IDR1,345.7bn, so the second half neither builds nor releases working capital, and no release is assumed in the year the filing shows the opposite [S3, F40, F41].

The cash roll ties to the June actual only after the working-capital definition is allowed for. From the FY2025 cash of IDR78.4bn the model adds profit, depreciation and the first-half borrowing and subtracts capex, the working-capital build and the small distribution, giving FY2026E cash of IDR102.9bn; that is a few tens of billions above the IDR65.2bn of cash on hand at 30 June, because the second half neither builds nor releases [S3, F48]. The balance-sheet build of IDR383.2bn is larger than the cash-flow build the same filings show, because the operating working-capital line contains restricted funds and prepaid tax that the cash-flow statement does not treat as an operating use; we keep the reported balance-sheet definition, disclose that it is the more conservative of the two, and note that the valuation takes its cash and debt from the 30 June balance sheet rather than from this forecast cash line [S3]. FY2026E net debt of IDR1,464.0bn is therefore within a few tens of billions of the June position rather than the hundreds of billions below it that the previous version carried, which is what the challenge on the cash roll was about.

The balance sheet is levered and short-dated. At the end of FY2025 debt was IDR1,340.7bn, cash IDR78.4bn and equity IDR1,777.0bn, and the June 2026 LK shows borrowing higher again [S4, S0, S3]. The structure is the problem: short-term bank loans were IDR1,016.6bn at 30 June 2026, up by nearly a third in six months and nearly two thirds of gross borrowings, against liquid resources that are a fraction of the maturing lines [S3]. The dividend appropriates FY2024 profit at Rp8 a share, just under half of it, with no FY2025 dividend resolved at the annual report date; we model that ratio rather than a cut and the balance sheet carries the difference [S2, p79, F20, S4].

Earnings quality is the second leg. The 2026 profit is operating, not below the line — there is no fair-value gain carrying the result — but the associate income inside operating profit has to be stripped out to see it, and the film business earned IDR129.9bn less IDR4.4bn before net finance in the half year [S3, F12, F36]. The cash flow does not support the profit: operating cash flow was IDR208.1bn in FY2024 and IDR221.2bn in FY2025 on net profit of IDR10.6bn and IDR12.7bn, an accruals ratio of about minus six per cent of average total assets in each year [S4, p19]. In the first half of 2026 the sign reverses: operating cash flow was a use of IDR-146.7bn against net profit of IDR66.2bn, about plus five and a half per cent, because trade receivables rose to IDR968.8bn from a year-end level more than half as low again and advances rose to IDR56.8bn from almost nothing [S3, p4 and p9]. The forecast carries that working-capital intensity rather than assuming a release in the year the filing shows the opposite [S4, S3].

One reconciling item is left open, and it is a book-equity question, not a valuation one. The associate note shows the carrying amount derecognised on the January sale as about three fifths of the IDR114.9bn received, which implies a disposal result of roughly two fifths of the proceeds, yet that result is in neither the printed pre-tax profit nor the equity movement: total comprehensive income of IDR164.1bn is profit of IDR66.2bn plus an exchange movement equal to the rise in the translation reserve to IDR534.7bn [S3, F42, F43, F44]. It cannot change the valuation. The IDR114.9bn of proceeds is already inside the 30 June cash and therefore in net debt, and the retained stake is already marked at the sale price in the bridge, so adding the gain to enterprise value would count the same proceeds twice [S3, F37, F38]. Where it sits is an audit item for the FY2026 accounts: recognising it would lift reported book equity only, and we do not credit it to earnings or to value [S3].

We value Argha on a discounted cash flow of the operating business and give the multiples no weight in the target, but we now show the peer set and argue the discount rather than assert that the screens are distorted: the trailing PE of 31.4x uses trough earnings and the forward PE of 3.0x a spike year [S0, S3].

On the covered chemical set the comparison is not like for like. ADMG trades on a book multiple two thirds above Argha's and the pack carries no EBITDA multiple for it; APLI carries an EBITDA multiple several times Argha's on a book multiple several times higher [S0]. Two things the screens do not show explain the gap. Argha's EV/EBITDA of 4.2x is on a spike year's EBITDA of IDR443.6bn. The multiple table uses one enterprise-value definition throughout: the market capitalisation at Rp650 a share plus the modelled net debt of the year in question, so the balance sheet moves with the denominator — IDR1,262.3bn in FY2025, IDR1,464.0bn in FY2026E and IDR1,357.8bn in FY2027E. On that definition FY2025A is 6.3x and FY2027E 4.5x [S0, S3]. And the book of IDR1,936.0bn contains a translation reserve of IDR534.7bn, about a quarter of it, so the clean price-to-book is higher than the 0.2x the screen shows [S3, F42, F43]. The apparent cheapness is leverage and a reserve, not value: with net debt several times the market capitalisation, the equity multiple on normal earnings is the one that matters, and it is not low.

The discount rate is the house build with one correction. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2%, the country risk premium 2.5% and the industry unlevered beta 0.90; at the capped debt-to-equity ratio of 2.00 the levered beta is 2.30, giving a cost of equity of 15.5% and a WACC of 10.1% [S4]. The correction is to the cost of debt: the engine prices it at 9.4% while the company pays about 5.8% on dollar trade lines, and because debt is two thirds of the structure that gap overstates WACC by about two percentage points; we offset it through the cost of equity rather than editing the deck, and the assumptions note sets out the arithmetic [S4, S3]. The same cost of equity rolls the target forward, so the correction lowers the roll factor, and we disclose the direction rather than claim the higher figure [S4].

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR1,223.5bn [S4]. Against the 30 June 2026 balance sheet it falls short of net debt: short-term bank loans of IDR1,016.6bn, current maturities of IDR21.8bn and long-term borrowings of IDR528.4bn, less cash on hand of IDR65.2bn and short-term investments of IDR12.8bn, leave the lenders ahead of the enterprise value [S3]. Two sourced corrections turn that deficit into a small positive equity. First, the associate: the engine carries IDR100.4bn of book value and we add the mark to the observable sale price, which values the retained stake above book and is the difference the challenge asked us to evidence [S3, F37, F38, F52]. Second, the half-year stub: the first row of the DCF table discounts the full-year cash flow by the part of the year left after 30 June, which is the wrong measure when the working-capital build is all in the first half, and the bridge restores the second half that the stub omits [S3, F35, F40, F41]. Together with the associate book value they give base equity of Rp109 a share. The valuation date is 13 November 2026: because the cash-flow stub starts at the 30 June 2026 balance sheet, the first DCF row counts the part of FY2026E remaining after that date at time zero, and the twelve-month target rolls the base value one year from 13 November 2026 at the cost of equity before deducting the distribution, so it is dated November 2027 [S3, S4]. Rolling that forward at the 15.5% cost of equity and deducting the Rp101 distribution gives the twelve-month base case of Rp25 [S3, S0]. The terminal value carries about 51.7% of the enterprise value, so the value depends on the terminal spread, held at the FY2025 audited level rather than the 2026 peak [S4].
Capex is 3.9% of revenue in FY2026E, the first-half run-rate, and 5.5% from FY2027E, the restated depreciation rate, so the terminal year reinvests what it consumes [S3, p9, S4].

The cross-checks disagree with the DCF and with each other, and the disagreement is the finding. On the single definition above the stock is at 4.2x FY2026E EBITDA and 4.5x FY2027E, and on price-to-book at 0.2x reported book [S0, S3]. The engine pairs the market capitalisation with the modelled FY2026E net debt of IDR1,464.0bn; on the 30 June actual, with the borrowings of IDR1,016.6bn, IDR21.8bn and IDR528.4bn less cash of IDR65.2bn and short-term investments of IDR12.8bn, the multiple is a fraction of a turn higher, and the June balance sheet is the one we quote [S3]. The book multiple needs care: equity attributable to owners was IDR1,936.0bn at 30 June 2026 and the translation reserve within it was IDR534.7bn, so the clean P/B is higher than the screen shows [S3, F42, F43]. The engine's multiple methods use FY2025 trough earnings and floor at zero, so we give them no weight [S4, S3, S0].

The sensitivity grid is the map of the risk, and it is steeper than a target of Rp90 suggests. Half a point higher on the WACC takes the base value from Rp109 to nothing, while half a point lower more than doubles it and a point lower takes it to more than four times the base, because the enterprise value sits near net debt and the equity is a thin sliver. A point of gross margin above base takes the twelve-month value to many times the target and two points to more than ten times it, while a point below base is already nil (fund record sensitivity grids).

What the price implies. The engine's reverse DCF does not bracket this name, so we decompose the gap on the balance sheet [S4]. At Rp650 the market capitalisation is IDR398.0bn; adding the June borrowings of IDR1,016.6bn, IDR21.8bn and IDR528.4bn and deducting cash of IDR65.2bn and short-term investments of IDR12.8bn gives an enterprise value, and net of the associate at the sale price it is about two fifths above the DCF's IDR1,223.5bn on a like-for-like basis [S0, S3, F37, F38]. That premium needs a terminal reported gross margin a shade above the FY2022 peak, the margin no filed note supports [S2, F32, S4]. The earlier version compared the associate-inclusive market value with the associate-exclusive DCF and overstated the implied margin; on the corrected basis the market is not pricing the peak itself, it is pricing a spread slightly better than the peak and holding it for ever.

The scenario values frame the answer. Base is Rp25 at half the weight, the bear Rp0 at three tenths and the bull Rp435 at a fifth, weighting to about Rp100 before the liquidity discount and a target of Rp90 [S0, S4]. The target is mostly the bull case: the bear leaves nothing because the enterprise value falls below net debt, and the base is a small positive after the distribution. The asymmetry is leverage, not a modelling artefact: the base equity is small against the debt, so a small change in the enterprise value is a large change in the per-share value, and the bull case is close to where the stock trades today [S0, S3, S4].

**Feedstock reversal (high likelihood, high impact).** The margin is a mark-up on a polymer price set by naphtha, which rose by most of its value in the year to the autumn [S6]. If resin falls faster than film the mark-up compresses and the gross margin returns to the FY2024-FY2025 level of about a tenth [S4].

**Leverage and refinancing (medium likelihood, high impact).** The debt is short-dated: IDR1,016.6bn of short-term bank loans at 30 June 2026, nearly two thirds of gross borrowings, up by nearly a third in six months [S3, p5]. The facilities are annually renewable trade finance, so the roll is the event, and we hold gross debt flat because free cash flow would not fund repayment after a half-of-profit dividend [S3, S4, F20]. We do not run the refinancing as a separate scenario shock, and the reason is mechanical: the DCF is unlevered, so a higher cost of debt moves the interest line, the earnings and the distribution, not the enterprise value the target is built on, and the bear is already at zero because the enterprise value falls below the June net debt [S4, S3]. The risk is carried in that zero floor and in the recovery the base assumes, not in a discount-rate shock that would double-count it.
**Demand and export (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Just under half of first-half sales were exports, so a weaker global consumer or a stronger rupiah would reduce volume and mix [S3, S2].

**Capacity execution (medium likelihood, medium impact).** A delay to the CPP line pushes out the volume and mix the forecast assumes; it is small against the group, but it is the only growth capex [S2, S4].

**Policy (medium likelihood, medium impact, two-sided).** The zero import duty runs for six months; its expiry raises landed feedstock cost, and it is likely to be extended while the spike lasts and to lapse when it does [S5].

**Associate disposal (low likelihood, high impact).** The retained stake is saleable and the company has already sold part of it once [S3, F38, F52]. A further sale at the same price is neutral to value because the bridge already marks it there; a sale below it, or a loss of associate status that forces the carrying value back to the group's share of net assets, is a bear-case event. Because the forecast already excludes associate income, the value of a disposal is the observable price for what is sold and the DCF does not change [S3, F36].

**Governance and related parties (low likelihood, medium impact).** The three controlling holders own most of the shares and the float is thin; we found no improper transaction, but a related-party deal or capital action favouring the controlling group is the route for minority value transfer [S2, S4].

**Liquidity (high likelihood, medium impact).** The stock trades IDR537.3m a day on a three-month window to 12 November 2026 and the free float is under a fifth of the shares [S0]. That discount is the one input that moved the previous version: the measured traded value is just above the half-billion-rupiah tier that sets a tenth rather than a fifth. The pack carries no usable volume series, so we cannot decompose the crossing into price and volume; because rupiah value is shares times price and the price rose over the window, part of the crossing is a price effect [S0]. If the measure falls back below the tier the discount returns to a fifth, which takes a further tenth off the pre-discount value of Rp100 rather than changing the fundamental view.

The bear case takes revenue growth four points below base and the gross margin a point and a half below, so the spread normalises faster than the deck assumes while the debt stays on the balance sheet [S4, S3]; the reported margin ends between the FY2023 trough and the FY2024 level rather than at the trough itself, which is the correction the challenge asked for, and the equity floors at zero because the enterprise value falls below net debt, not because the company is insolvent [S3]. The base case is the FY2025 audited margin on the house deck, leaving Rp109 a share before the distribution and a twelve-month value of Rp25 [S3, S4]. The bull mirrors the bear: four points more growth and a point and a half more margin as the CPP line ramps and the mix improves [S2, S3]. The base takes half the weight, the bear three tenths and the bull a fifth, because the first half supports a good FY2026 but the cash-flow statement and the maturity wall make the bear at least as likely as the bull [S3, S4].

The signposts that would change our view: the third-quarter gross margin, which tells us whether the pass-through held after the June peak; the net-debt trajectory; the CPP line start-up; the extension or expiry of the import-duty relief; and any related-party or capital action [S3, S5, S2].

Ownership is concentrated and stable. PT Tiara Intimahkota holds 36.1%, PT Prismatama Nugraha 27.3% and PT Nawa Panduta 15.1%, with management holding a small stake and the public the balance [S2]. The three are related to the founding family and act together, so the free float is less than a fifth and minorities have little influence over capital allocation [S0, S2]. Related-party dealings are small: sales to related parties were a rounding item of first-half revenue and no material related-party purchase or asset transaction is disclosed [S3, S4]. We found no pledged-share disclosure, material legal case, sanction or special notation, and the EY member firm issued an unqualified opinion on the FY2025 accounts [S2, S3, S4].

The dividend record is a distribution of the prior year's profit, not a policy. The AGM appropriated FY2024 profit and paid Rp8 a share during 2025, just under half of profit attributable, and no FY2025 dividend had been resolved at the annual report date [S2, p79, F20]. The model follows the filing's timing: each distribution is paid in the year after the profit that funds it, so the FY2026E distribution of Rp101 a share is paid out of FY2027E, when free cash flow to equity is IDR167.8bn and cash rises to IDR209.1bn [S4, S3]. That is a cover of about two and a half times, and the distribution actually paid during FY2026E is the prior year's IDR5.1bn, which the FY2026E free cash flow to equity of IDR29.5bn covers. The challenge's point stands on the quoted target, not on the economics: the twelve-month price deducts the Rp101 distribution and the total return adds it back, so the rating is invariant to the split, and before the deduction the base twelve-month value would be Rp109 compounded at the 15.5% cost of equity. We disclose both rather than claim a dividend the balance sheet cannot fund and a target that hides it.

Governance has one open flag, the disposal result. The associate note implies a gain on the January sale that is in neither the printed profit nor the equity movement, as the financial section sets out, and we do not credit it [S3, F38, F44]. The associate is treated as a saleable, non-core asset rather than a permanent bridge item: it is marked at an observable transaction price, the retained interest is below the level at which significant influence is presumed, and a further disposal would be valued the same way, at the price the next buyer pays rather than at book [S3, F37, F38, F52].

On ESG the exposures are those of a polymer converter: energy use, solvent handling, and the end-of-life profile of plastic packaging [S2]. The governance score is held back by the controlling group, the thin float and the leveraged balance sheet [S2, S0].

The nearest catalyst is the third-quarter 2026 financial statements, expected in the current quarter, which will show whether the gross margin held after the June peak and whether the borrowing increase reversed [S3]. The FY2026 audited results follow in the first quarter of 2027 with the dividend proposal, and the annual general meeting in the second; the audited accounts are also where the disposal result has to appear [S2, S4]. The CPP line has no disclosed completion date, so its start-up announcement is the first read on the mix the forecast assumes [S2].

The KPIs we monitor are the gross margin; revenue to raw-material cost, which tests the pass-through; net debt and interest cover; the export share; CPP progress and metallising mix; and the import-duty relief with any change in the oil or rupiah decks [S4, S3, S2, S5]. What would make us wrong on the upside is the spike persisting into 2027, a faster CPP ramp or an extension of the duty relief, and on the downside a sharp fall in the film price relative to resin, a refinancing squeeze or a related-party use of cash [S5, S6, S3, S2]. We would revisit the rating on any of these, and on the third-quarter accounts.

bear.narrative: The feedstock spike reverses faster than selling prices: Brent falls to the deck long-run anchor by FY2027E while customers refuse the price increases already quoted, so the unpassed cost becomes a 15% leak and the reported gross margin ends at about 9.5%, between the FY2023 trough of 8.26% and the FY2024 level of 10.33% - the 1.5-point shock actually run, not a return to the trough. Export demand weakens as the rupiah stays firm, the CPP line starts into a soft market, and the 19% revenue jump of 2026 is a one-year restock that unwinds. Equity is nil not because the margin alone destroys it but because the enterprise value falls below the IDR 1,488.8bn of 30 June net debt; the IDR 1,016.6bn of short-term lines are renewed at higher rates, a cost that moves the interest line, the earnings and the distribution rather than the unlevered enterprise value, so it is narrated here and does not change the zero.

bull.narrative: The feedstock spike persists into 2027 and the converter keeps recovering it in price, so revenue holds above IDR 3.5tn and the margin settles at 14% rather than tapering to the four-year average; the CPP line ramps quickly, metallised and high-barrier film take a larger share of the mix, and export volumes grow as Southeast Asian converters consolidate. The zero import duty is extended, the through-cycle margin is 1.5 points above base, and the associate is held at the observable sale price rather than re-rated.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +19.0%: first-half 2026 net sales were IDR 1,754.8bn against IDR 1,454.6bn a year earlier (+20.6%) [S3, F10], and the second quarter alone was the stronger at IDR 1,034.2bn [S3], so annualising the first half gives IDR 3,509.6bn, +19.4% on FY2025. We hold +19.0%, allowing for the feedstock spike to ease in the fourth quarter as Brent rolls from the 96.0 deck average toward 84.0. FY2027E -6.0%: the deck takes Brent from 96.0 to 84.0 (-12.5%), and on the 71.5% of COGS that is oil-linked and the roughly 95% of the raw-material move that reaches the selling price [S4, F15] the selling-price deflation is about 8.5 points, offset by roughly 2.5 points of volume growth from the new CPP line (7,200 t) coming on stream [S2, F25]. FY2028E +3.0% with Brent at 80.0, then +4.0% a year in FY2029E-FY2030E as Indonesian flexible-packaging demand grows and the CPP line fills; the long-run rate is 4.0%, the same as the DCF terminal growth, and it is below the nominal GDP growth the macro deck implies for an Indonesian rupiah reporter [S0].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The input is the margin at FY2025 feedstock prices (the template's base period), so the Brent link below is the only thing that moves it. First-half 2026 printed 13.02% (gross profit IDR 228.4bn on IDR 1,754.8bn of sales) against 10.14% in first-half 2025 and 11.02% for FY2025 [S3, F11, F10, S2, F32]. That half-year is the calibration point: FY2026E is set at 14.3% at base input costs, which the model's Brent link takes to about 13.0% reported, reproducing the print [S3]; the engine prints 13.04%. The half-year margin is not a through-cycle margin and we do not carry it into perpetuity. The audited record is 12.08% in FY2022, 8.26% in FY2023, 10.33% in FY2024 and 11.02% in FY2025, a four-year average of about 10.4% [S0, S2, F32], and no filed note quantifies the margin uplift from metallised or CPP film: the annual report says only that the Metalizing 5 and CPP project is expected to improve production-process efficiency and that the board encourages premium product sales, which is a direction, not a number [S2]. We therefore taper the input from 14.3% in FY2026E to 11.8% by FY2030E and 11.8% in the long run, which with the Brent link on a long-run Brent about a quarter above the FY2025 base prints a reported margin of 11.04% in FY2035E: exactly the FY2025 audited 11.02% and below the FY2022 peak of 12.08%, so the terminal is anchored on the last actual and not on the peak. The mix shift gets no credit in the base beyond that anchor; it is the bull case, and it is carried there as 1.5 points above base.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Raw materials used were IDR 1,869.7bn of IDR 2,614.9bn of cost of goods sold in FY2025, 71.5% [S4, F15, F3]. The two inputs are polypropylene and PET chip, both oil-derived, so essentially the whole raw-material line is Brent-exposed; direct labour and production expenses (utilities, consumables) are the remaining 28.5% and are only indirectly linked. We use 71.5%, not a round 70%, because the note gives the exact split and the first-half 2026 evidence (revenue +20.6%, cost of goods sold +16.8%) is consistent with the full raw-material line moving with the feedstock [S3, F10].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: This parameter is the fraction of a feedstock move that is recovered in the selling price, so (1 - pass) is the margin leak the company absorbs; it is calibrated on the margin, not on revenue, and revenue is a separate driver above. The calibration is the first half of 2026: the base-input margin of 14.3% falls to 13.04% in FY2026E on a Brent average 40.9% above the FY2025 base of 68.1, a leak of 1.26 points of revenue on 0.715 x 40.9 = 29.3 points of feedstock cost, which is 4.3% of the feedstock move, i.e. a pass-through of about 95.7% [S3, S4]. We set 95%, the round number the identity supports. The 5% residual is the timing and inventory leak on polymer bought before the price rise. Note what this parameter does NOT do: it does not set revenue, so the 20.6% revenue growth on a 42.8% polypropylene move is not evidence about it [S5].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Selling expenses of IDR 72.6bn plus general and administrative expenses of IDR 39.3bn were IDR 111.9bn in first-half 2026, 6.4% of revenue before other operating income; net of the IDR 9.1bn other operating income the charge was 5.86% [S3]. FY2025 selling plus G&A was IDR 215.6bn, 7.3% of revenue [S4]. The cost is largely fixed in rupiah (the company employed 1,006 people at end-2025 [S2, F31]), so the ratio falls as the 2026 revenue base rises. FY2026E is set at 5.86%, the film-only ratio that turns the annualised first-half gross profit into the film-only operating profit of IDR 125.6bn a half (IDR 251.2bn a year) [S3, F12, F36]. The earlier 5.6% was the ratio that reproduced the printed IDR 129.9bn operating profit, but that print already contains IDR 4.37bn of associate income; using it imported about IDR 9bn a year of Stenta earnings into EBIT and counted the stake again in the bridge. The ratio then drifts back to 6.2%-6.4% as revenue deflates with Brent in FY2027E-FY2028E.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK: depreciation was IDR 164.8bn in FY2025 and IDR 153.0bn in FY2024, split IDR 160.1bn production, IDR 3.8bn G&A and IDR 0.9bn selling [S4, F8, F9], against the data pack's IDR 4.7bn, which is only a fragment of the charge. First-half 2026 depreciation was IDR 96.4bn [S3, F14], an annual rate of about IDR 193bn. On the FY2026E revenue base of IDR 3,497bn that is 5.5%, and we hold 5.5% because capex has been running above depreciation (the CPP line and metallising capacity) and the asset base is still growing [S4, F16].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: The first half is the only current evidence and it is a cash number: first-half 2026 capex was IDR 45.3bn of fixed-asset acquisitions plus IDR 22.8bn of advances for fixed-asset purchases, IDR 68.1bn [S3, p.9], against net sales of IDR 1,754.8bn [S3, F10], a 3.9% run-rate that annualises to IDR 136.2bn on the FY2026E base. That is the ratio we use for FY2026E. We do not step it up in the second half because no payment schedule, capital commitment or completion date is disclosed: the fixed-asset note says only that the advances went to several suppliers for machinery, equipment and building construction services, with an outstanding balance of IDR 31.6bn at 30 June 2026 [S3, note 14], and the annual report says the 7,200 t CPP facility is still under construction without giving a completion date [S2, F25]. For comparison, FY2025 was IDR 284.4bn of fixed-asset purchases plus IDR 62.7bn of advances, IDR 347.0bn or 11.8% of revenue [S4, F16, F17], so the first-half rate is a real step down from the expansion year and not a data artefact. From FY2027E capex is held at 5.5% of revenue, which is the restated depreciation rate [S4, F8], and it stays there: with no disclosed second project the most likely path is that the company reinvests what it consumes, and holding the 3.9% run-rate for ever would understate the maintenance requirement of a 4.0% nominal growth rate [S2, S4].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Rebased to the 30 June 2026 balance sheet, 38.48% of revenue, because the FY2025 ratio no longer describes the company the forecast starts from. On the model's definition (receivables, other receivables, inventories, prepaid expenses, advances, restricted funds and prepaid tax, less trade and other payables, taxes payable and accruals) operating working capital was IDR 962.5bn at 31 December 2025, 32.75% of FY2025 sales of IDR 2,938.7bn [S0, F1]; the 30 June 2026 balance sheet shows IDR 1,345.6bn on the same definition, which is 38.48% of the FY2026E revenue base of IDR 3,497.1bn [S3]. The build is cash-backed, not an accounting artefact: trade receivables rose from IDR 638.6bn to IDR 968.8bn (+51.8% against revenue +20.6%) and advances from IDR 3.1bn to IDR 56.8bn, and net cash used in operating activities was IDR 146.7bn against positive IDR 63.9bn a year earlier [S3, F40, F41, F35]. Applying 38.48% to FY2026E sets full-year operating working capital at the June level, i.e. NO second-half build and NO second-half release; the previous 32.75% set it at IDR 1,145.3bn, below the June balance, and so assumed a IDR 200bn release in a year whose first half was the largest working-capital build in the company's recent record. Note two components the pack's line carries that are not revenue-driven: restricted funds of IDR 80.0bn and prepaid tax of IDR 142.9bn at 30 June 2026 [S3]; both are held at the June proportion rather than released, and the cash-flow statement's own operating build of IDR 309.3bn is correspondingly about IDR 74bn smaller than the balance-sheet build of IDR 383.2bn used here. The ratio is held flat through the forecast and in the terminal year because no filing discloses a change in payment terms, a factoring arrangement or a receivable-sale programme [S2, S3, S4].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: First-half 2026 tax was IDR 24.2bn on pre-tax profit of IDR 90.4bn, 26.8% [S3], above the 22% statutory rate because of non-deductible items and the associate's tax. FY2025's effective rate was distorted by the low pre-tax base. We use 25.0%, between the statutory rate and the measured first-half rate, through the forecast and in the terminal year. There is no material tax shield: the group is profitable and has no disclosed accumulated-loss carryforward of the size that changed ADMG's rate.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Finance expense was IDR 70.2bn in FY2025 on opening debt of IDR 1,340.7bn, 5.2% [S4, F18, S0], and IDR 39.8bn in first-half 2026, an annual rate of about IDR 79.5bn against an average balance of about IDR 1,454bn, 5.5% [S3]. The 5.8% we use is inside the contractual range the accounts disclose: the short-term bank loans carry 5.40%-7.00% on the US dollar facilities, which are IDR 549.0bn of the IDR 1,016.6bn short-term total, and 6.29%-8.50% on the rupiah facilities [S3, note 16]. It is below the rupiah risk-free rate because most of the debt is dollar debt and the Company's functional currency is the US dollar, so the rupiah risk-free rate is not the opportunity cost of that borrowing; the relevant benchmark for a dollar facility is the dollar rate [S3, S4]. The marginal rate has risen with the BI rate and the loans are short-dated, so we do not model a fall.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Finance income was IDR 0.56bn in FY2025 and IDR 0.27bn in first-half 2026 on a cash balance of the order of IDR 80bn [S4, F19, S3], about 0.7%: the cash is mostly rupiah operating balances, not a treasury portfolio. Held at 0.7%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The first half is an actual: debt rose from IDR 1,340.7bn at 31 December 2025 to IDR 1,566.8bn at 30 June 2026, a net increase of IDR 226.2bn, in a half in which operating cash flow was minus IDR 146.7bn and receivables rose 51.8% [S3, F35, F40]. FY2026E therefore takes +IDR 226.2bn, the measured first-half draw, and holds it for the second half on the view that the receivables build does not repeat at the same rate. That is deliberately not a repayment path: short-term bank loans were IDR 1,016.6bn, 65% of gross debt, and grew 29% in six months [S3], so the structure is annually renewable trade finance and we do not assume it is repaid. From FY2027E we hold gross debt flat: free cash flow after the dividend is thin in every forecast year (FY2027E is the peak at about IDR 207bn against a dividend of about IDR 67bn on the 47.22% payout restored from the audited FY2024 resolution), so a scheduled repayment path would drive the cash line negative and is not supported by any disclosed facility maturity schedule [S3, S4, S2, F20]. Holding debt flat is the neutral assumption that neither assumes the lines are repaid nor that they grow; the refinancing risk is carried in the bear scenario and in the maturity discussion, not in a repayment slope the filings do not disclose.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: The operating profit line already includes other operating income and expenses (first-half 2026 a net IDR 9.1bn gain [S3]). The associate's share of profit, IDR 4.37bn in first-half 2026, is presented on the face of the income statement ABOVE the operating-profit subtotal, contrary to the accounting-policy note: the segment note shows manufacturing operating profit of IDR 125.6bn plus the associate line of IDR 4.37bn equalling the IDR 129.9bn operating profit printed [S3, F12, F36]. We therefore keep the forecast operating profit on the film business only and do NOT add the associate profit back here: the forecast EBIT is gross profit less the operating-cost ratio, and that ratio is struck on the film business, so the associate enters the valuation once, through the marked value of the holding in the equity bridge [S3, F37]. Zero, so the model's FCFF is the film business only.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interests were nil in first-half 2026 and IDR 0.01bn in FY2025 [S3, S4]; the only consolidated subsidiary with a minority is small. Held at zero.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: We model the ratio the shareholders have actually approved, 47.22%. The AGM resolution of 11 June 2025 appropriated the FY2024 profit and distributed IDR 5,020,433,600 of cash dividends, about 47.22% of total net profit, IDR 8.20 a share [S2, F20]; no FY2025 dividend has yet been resolved and the company discloses no standing payout policy [S2, S3]. The record is not smooth (FY2022 paid a small dividend, FY2023 paid none and FY2024 paid 47.22%), so this is the only stated number and anchoring on it is the method-card behaviour; the capex and debt ask are real, which is why the alternative 30% is discussed in the report but not used. The controlling shareholders hold 78.44% combined [S2, F28, F29, F30] and have taken cash out in every year the profit allowed. Funding: the engine pays each year distribution in the following year cash flow, because dividends_paid is the prior-year dps times shares, so the FY2026E IDR 100.68 a share, IDR 61.6bn, is paid out of FY2027E, when free cash flow to equity is IDR 167.8bn and cash still rises from IDR 102.9bn to IDR 209.0bn; the FY2026E free cash flow to equity of IDR 29.5bn has only the IDR 5.1bn paid in 2026 to cover, and the IDR 226.2bn borrowing is what carries the working-capital build. The 12-month target deducts the IDR 61.6bn as an ex-dividend adjustment and the total return adds it back, so the rating is invariant to the split between price and distribution; section 4 discloses the value before the deduction. Funding the distribution from new debt instead would raise net debt one for one and lower the equity value, which is why the payout is disclosed rather than treated as a free option [S3, F20, S4].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 612,248,000 shares issued and no corporate action disclosed in the FY2025 annual report or the first-half 2026 LK [S2, S3]. The public float is 18.39% [S0], above the exchange's free-float floor, so no dilution or index event is modelled.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.0%: the macro deck carries Indonesian consumer-price inflation at 3.28% and real GDP growth at 5.29%, so nominal GDP grows at roughly 8.7%, and a flexible-packaging converter that grows with food and consumer volumes should not be given a real decline. 4.0% is CPI plus about three quarters of a point of real volume, below nominal GDP growth, and it is consistent with the long-run revenue growth in the forecast above. It is the top of the CHEMICALS peer range, and the sensitivity grid shows 1pp of terminal growth is worth about a fifth of the DCF value, so we state the choice rather than bury it [S0].

challenges.challenge: The DCF credits 50.4% of FY2026E FCFF (Rp34.5bn) as the post-30-June cash flow, but FY2026E FCFF of Rp68.4bn is a full-year figure built from annual ratios and is not reconciled to the reported H1: CFO -Rp146.7bn less capex of Rp68.1bn (F50+F51) is about -Rp214.8bn, or about -Rp185bn on the model's own FCFF definition after adding back after-tax interest. The annual forecast therefore implies H2 FCFF of about +Rp250bn, not Rp34.5bn: the DCF omits roughly Rp200-250bn of the first period, about Rp330-405/share or 5-6x the entire base equity value of Rp63. If Rp34.5bn is right instead, then FY2026E FCFF of Rp68.4bn is overstated by the same order and the forecast itself is wrong.
challenges.answer: FY2026E working capital rebased to the 30 June balance sheet (38.48% of revenue, IDR 1,345.7bn), so the whole IDR 383.2bn build is first-half and the second half neither builds nor releases; a sourced valuation.bridge line of IDR 195.2bn adds the second-half FCFF the 50.4% stub omits (H1 FCFF -260.6 on the model definition, FY2026E -131.9, so H2 +128.7 against the -66.5 counted); base equity rises to IDR 120.4 a share and the target is rerun at IDR 95 [S3, F35, F40, F41].

challenges.challenge: The 10.25% Stenta sale is absent from the report: SPA of 21 Jan 2026 with Mega First Corporation Berhad at RM1.28/share, 21,153,578 shares for RM27.14m = Rp114.9bn, received 9 Feb 2026 (S3 note 13, p46). It prices the retained 12.5% at about Rp140bn (114.9/10.25x12.5) against the Rp100.4bn book that is the entire difference between the Rp38.5bn base equity value and a deficit. The carrying value derecognised was Rp69.3bn, so the filing implies a roughly Rp45.6bn excess that appears in neither the H1 P&L (pre-tax Rp90.4bn = operating profit 129.9 less net finance 39.5) nor equity (attributable equity +159.0bn vs total comprehensive income 164.1bn).
challenges.answer: Stenta retained 12.5% marked at the 21 January 2026 SPA price of RM1.283 a share (printed RM1,283) by a IDR 39.8bn bridge line to IDR 140.2bn against IDR 100.4bn book; the implied IDR 45.6bn disposal excess is disclosed in sections 3 and 6 as an unresolved reconciling item and is not credited [S3, F37, F38, F52].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the price implies 'a terminal gross margin at or above the FY2022 peak'. Net of the associate the market EV is Rp1,786bn against the DCF's Rp1,426.7bn, a 25% premium; the report's own sensitivity grid gives Rp738 of twelve-month value per 1pp of gross margin, so 25% needs about 0.8pp, i.e. roughly 11.8% terminal versus the 12.08% FY2022 peak. The 'at or above' claim only holds by comparing the associate-inclusive market EV (Rp1,887bn) with the associate-exclusive DCF, and the analyst's own extreme_call justification says 'near the FY2022 peak', not at or above.
challenges.answer: Premium and implied margin restated like-for-like: market EV net of the associate at the SPA price is IDR 1,747bn against the DCF's IDR 1,226.9bn, about two fifths above, implying a terminal reported margin a shade above the FY2022 peak; the sentence that compared an associate-inclusive market EV with an associate-exclusive DCF is corrected [S0, S3, F32].

challenges.challenge: The base case is floored at zero by subtracting a Rp105.9 dividend from a Rp72.6 twelve-month value, yet section 6 states no FY2025 dividend had been resolved at the annual report date, the H1 operating cash flow was -Rp146.7bn and the model's own gross debt is held flat. A Rp106 distribution is 1.7x the base equity value and unfunded; it is not the most likely path. Without it the base twelve-month value is about Rp73 and the target about Rp159.
challenges.answer: Disclosed that the model pays each distribution a year after the profit that funds it (FY2026E dps IDR 105.9, IDR 64.9bn, is paid in FY2027E where FCFE is IDR 167.9bn, about 2.6x cover), that the target deducts it as an ex-dividend adjustment and the total return adds it back, and the value before the deduction (IDR 120.4 at the 15.5% COE); the payout stays at the approved 47.22% [S2, F20, S4].

challenges.challenge: The bear shocks only revenue growth -4pp and gross margin -1.5pp and omits the refinancing/cost-of-debt shock that section 5 calls medium-likelihood/high-impact and 'the roll is the event' (Rp1,016.6bn short-term loans, 65% of borrowings, annually renewable). Its narrative says the margin returns to the FY2023 trough of 8.26% (F32), but a -1.5pp shock takes the reported terminal margin to about 9.5%; the zero comes from leverage, not the stated shock.
challenges.answer: Bear narrative now matches the -1.5pp margin shock actually run (terminal margin between the FY2023 trough and FY2024, not the trough); the refinancing shock is excluded with the mechanism stated: the DCF is unlevered, so a higher cost of debt moves interest, earnings and the distribution, not enterprise value, and the bear is already at zero on the June net debt [S3, S4].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E net debt of Rp1,256.8bn is Rp232bn below the 30 June actual of Rp1,488.8bn: the model has unrestricted cash rising from Rp65.2bn to Rp310.1bn in the second half of a year whose H1 operating cash flow was -Rp146.7bn. FY2026E delta-NWC of Rp182.8bn against an H1 build of roughly Rp309bn (NP 66.2 + DA 96.4 - CFO 146.7) implies an H2 working-capital release of about Rp126bn, contradicting section 3's 'the forecast carries that working-capital intensity rather than assuming a release'. The reported EV/EBITDA cross-check (3.7x FY2026E, 4.0x FY2027E) uses this Rp1,256.8bn; on the H1 balance sheet it is 4.2x and 4.9x.
challenges.answer: FY2026E working capital pinned to the 30 June balance sheet so the second half neither builds nor releases; the cash roll is reconciled to the June actual with the balance-sheet versus cash-flow working-capital difference (restricted funds, prepaid tax) disclosed; FY2026E net debt of IDR 1,457.2bn is now close to the June IDR 1,488.8bn, and the multiple cross-check is restated on the 30 June balance sheet [S3, F39, F46, F47, F48, F49].

challenges.challenge: The restatement paragraph reads 'The data pack carries depreciation of IDR164.8bn for FY2025, a fragment of the charge; the fixed-asset note shows IDR164.8bn' - both halves cannot be true. The assumptions note says the pack carried IDR4.7bn and the note shows IDR164.8bn (F8, S4); the report has the wrong pack figure in the first clause.
challenges.answer: Corrected: the data pack carried a depreciation charge of only a few billion rupiah against the fixed-asset note's IDR 164.8bn for FY2025 and IDR 153.0bn for FY2024; the sentence no longer prints the note figure twice [S4, F8, F9].

challenges.challenge: 'The associate contribution of IDR4.4bn sits outside operating profit' is contradicted by S3 p6: 228.4 gross profit + 4.37 associate - 72.6 selling - 39.3 G&A + 9.09 other = 129.9 operating profit. The FY2025 audited P&L is the same (operating profit 97.7 includes the 12.97 associate line, S4 p16). The earnings-quality claim that 'the 2026 profit is operating, not below the line' therefore overstates clean operating profit by 3.4% in H1 and the FY2025 comparison by 13%.
